entries.title: Picked the engine and wrote the bootstrap prompt in a separate Claude chat
entries.body:
Before any code, a claude.ai conversation compared engines for a phone-first browser jam game and settled on **Phaser 3 from a CDN, no build step**, deployed on Netlify. It also drafted the bootstrap prompt that started the first Claude Code session.

That prompt was cut off when it was pasted: everything after "Placeholder art is drawn in" got lost. The missing rules were added later in the Claude Code session.

*Lightly condensed by Quirin: a superseded GitHub Pages version of the prompt is reduced to a one-line note.*

conversation.q: What's the best framework for a game jam with Claude? I want to run and iterate in the browser, primarily on my phone, maybe also a laptop. Not sure about the engine.
conversation.a:
Phaser, delivered as a single HTML file that pulls Phaser from a CDN, is the best fit.

**Why this combination works**
- **No build step.** One self-contained HTML page, published and opened on the phone right away. Each change is edited and republished to the same link; you reload. No toolchain, no local server, no laptop required.
- **Phaser is well-trodden ground.** Mature, well documented, with lots of example code, so Claude is reliable with it. It covers what jam games need: sprites, tilemaps, arcade physics, tweens, particles, sound, cameras, scene management.
- **It handles phones properly.** Built-in touch/pointer input, and a scale manager that fits and letterboxes the game to any screen.

**Alternatives depending on the game**
- **Plain Canvas / vanilla JS** for very small or abstract games (puzzles, one-button games). Less to learn, but you rebuild basics like collision yourself.
- **KAPLAY** (formerly Kaboom.js) for tiny arcade games; quicker and more playful than Phaser, smaller ecosystem.
- **Three.js** if the game needs to be 3D. Same single-file/CDN workflow, but 3D costs much more jam time.
- **Godot** is a great engine but doesn't fit this workflow: editor on a laptop and a web export for every iteration.

**Tips**
- Design for touch from minute one (tap/swipe, big hit areas, decide portrait vs. landscape early).
- Use generated or placeholder art (shapes, emoji, art drawn in code).
- Iterate in small changes after each playtest.
- Keep state in memory, not browser storage.

conversation.q: Give me a prompt to bootstrap the repo for this with Phaser.
conversation.a: *(First version targeted GitHub Pages; superseded by the Netlify version below.)*

Only a few lines change, since a no-build repo works on Netlify as-is: swap the Pages workflow for a `netlify.toml` (publish = ".", no build command, no-cache headers), update the README note, and drop the Pages setup step.

To connect it in Netlify: "Add new site" → "Import from Git" → pick the repo. It reads netlify.toml, so leave the build command empty. Every push to main deploys to your `*.netlify.app` URL. Pull requests get deploy previews, so a change on a branch can be playtested at its own URL before merging.

conversation.q: Give me a new prompt for the bootstrap.
conversation.a:
**Final bootstrap prompt (paste into Claude Code):**

```
Bootstrap a game jam repo for a mobile-first browser game using Phaser 3, deployed on Netlify.

Constraints:
- No build step, no npm, no bundler. Plain ES modules served as static files.
- Load Phaser from a CDN (jsdelivr, pinned to a specific 3.x version) in index.html.
- Must run as-is on any static host, so use relative paths only.
- Phone is the primary target: touch controls first, keyboard as a bonus on laptop.

Structure:
- index.html: viewport meta (no zoom), full-screen canvas, Phaser script tag, loads src/main.js
- src/main.js: Phaser game config with Scale.FIT + CENTER_BOTH, a fixed logical resolution (portrait 720x1280 unless I say otherwise), arcade physics, and the scene list
- src/scenes/: BootScene (generates placeholder textures in code with Graphics, no image files), MenuScene (tap to start), GameScene (a tiny playable demo: a player that moves toward where you touch or drag, plus something to collect, plus a score), GameOverScene (tap to restart)
- src/config.js: tunable constants (speeds, sizes, colors) in one place, so I can ask for "feel" changes quickly
- assets/: empty folder with a .gitkeep, for later
- netlify.toml: publish = "." with no build command; add a header rule so index.html and src/** are served with Cache-Control: no-cache (so the phone always picks up the latest push)
- README.md: how to play locally (any static server, e.g. `python3 -m http.server`) and a note that Netlify deploys on push

Also create CLAUDE.md with working rules for future sessions:
- Keep it no-build and CDN-only. Don't add npm dependencies.
- Every change must keep the game playable on a phone. Touch input is the primary control scheme.
- Placeholder art is drawn in code unless I provide assets.
- Don't use localStorage for anything important.
- Put tunables in src/config.js, not inline.
- Make small, focused changes and commit each one with a clear message, so I can playtest after every push.
- After each change, tell me in one or two sentences what to test on the phone.

Finally, prevent the usual mobile pitfalls: block pull-to-refresh and double-tap zoom on the canvas, handle multi-touch, and pause the game when the tab is hidden.

When done, commit and push.
```

entries.title: Asked Google Gemini how a Pac-Man arcade machine works, layer by layer
entries.body:
In a separate Google Gemini chat, Quirin asked for the layers of tech in the original Pac-Man cabinet. Then he had Gemini order them from the screen inwards and map each one to a dot-collecting game mechanic. The result became the plan for the deeper layers (see `design/systems/emulator.md`). Some hardware facts in the answers are off (NMI instead of the maskable IM 2 interrupt, the Left input bit, the `0x4920` address); the corrections are in the design doc.

*Exported from the chat as a PDF and converted to text by Claude; line breaks and list formatting were reconstructed, wording unchanged. The time wasn't recorded.*

conversation.q: i want to understand layers of tech involved in an original pacman arcade machine.give me a list
conversation.a:
The architecture of the original 1980 Namco Pac-Man arcade machine relies on a strictly coupled hardware-software stack, operating entirely without a host operating system. The system employs memory-mapped I/O, where the execution of software logic causally drives hardware rendering and audio generation by mutating specific memory addresses.

Here is the deterministic stack, ordered from physical input to application logic:

1. Electromechanical Interface Layer (Input/Output)
- Mechanisms: Joystick assemblies and coin mechanisms utilize physical microswitches.
- Dependencies: Actuating a switch closes a circuit, pulling a specific input line low. The state of these lines is buffered through logic gates and mapped to specific memory addresses on the system bus.
2. CPU and System Bus Architecture
- Processor: Zilog Z80 8-bit microprocessor clocked at 3.072 MHz.
- System Bus: The Z80 interfaces with the rest of the board via a 16-bit address bus and an 8-bit data bus. The physical wiring of the address bus determines the strict memory map (where RAM, ROM, and I/O devices reside).
- Dependencies: The CPU fetches instructions sequentially from ROM via the data bus, manipulating local registers or writing back to RAM/I/O addresses.
3. Memory Hierarchy
- Program ROM: Read-only memory chips storing the immutable Z80 assembly instructions (the game engine and logic).
- Graphics/Audio ROM and PROMs: Separate chips storing the bitmapped tile data (characters and sprites), audio waveforms, and color lookup tables (palettes).
- Static RAM (SRAM): Volatile memory divided functionally by the software into Work RAM (game state, variable storage), Video RAM (VRAM, defining what is drawn on screen), and Color RAM.
4. Hardware Video Renderer
- Raster Timing Generator: Discrete TTL logic circuits that generate the horizontal (H-sync) and vertical (V-sync) synchronization signals necessary to drive the CRT monitor's electron beam.
2. Background Tile Engine: Dedicated hardware that continuously reads the VRAM array (a grid representing the screen). For each VRAM entry, it fetches the corresponding 8x8 pixel bitmap from Graphic ROM and the color assignment from Color RAM/PROM, generating the maze and static elements.
3. Hardware Sprites: A distinct hardware subsystem that overlays moving objects (Pac-Man, ghosts) on top of the background. The CPU writes an object's X/Y coordinates and tile ID to a designated memory range; the sprite hardware automatically handles the positioning and pixel rendering independently of CPU cycles.
5. Hardware Audio Subsystem
1. Namco WSG (Waveform Sound Generator): A custom sound chip driven by memory-mapped registers.
2. Dependencies: The CPU writes frequency, volume, and waveform index values to specific memory addresses. The WSG reads these registers, fetches the specified 4-bit waveform sample from a PROM, and outputs a digital signal to a Digital-to-Analog Converter (DAC) for amplification.
6. Bare-Metal Execution Control (Interrupts)
1. Mechanism: There is no scheduler or OS. System timing relies entirely on hardware interrupts.
2. Dependencies: When the video renderer finishes drawing a frame and the CRT beam returns to the top of the screen (the Vertical Blanking interval, or V-blank), the video hardware asserts a Non-Maskable Interrupt (NMI) on the Z80 CPU pin at precisely 60.6 Hz. This NMI forces the CPU to jump to the main game loop, ensuring the software logic executes at a deterministic framerate perfectly synchronized with the display hardware.
7. Application Logic (Software State Machines)
1. Input Polling: Software reads the memory-mapped input registers to update Pac-Man's trajectory variables.
2. State Machines (Ghost AI): Algorithms update the coordinate vectors for each ghost based on deterministic target-tile logic (Chase, Scatter, or Frightened states).
3. Collision Detection: The software checks for overlaps between coordinate variables (Pac-Man's bounding box vs. dots, power pellets, or ghosts) and mutates game state accordingly.
4. Rendering Update: The CPU pushes the updated X/Y coordinates of the sprites and any changes to the background tiles (e.g., an eaten dot being replaced by a blank space) into VRAM and Sprite RAM, which the hardware renderer will display on the subsequent CRT raster pass.

conversation.q: arrange this into a series of layers, by travelling through the system from the screen
conversation.a:
1. Analog Output Display (Cathode Ray Tube): The terminal endpoint of the causal chain. An electron beam performs a continuous raster sweep across a phosphor matrix, modulated by analog RGB voltage signals and strictly synchronized by discrete horizontal (H-sync) and vertical (V-sync) pulses to emit visible photons.
2. Hardware Signal Generation (Video/Audio Subsystems): Discrete TTL logic circuits and Digital-to-Analog Converters (DACs) output the analog voltages required by the CRT and speakers. Dedicated hardware compositors (the background tile engine and sprite hardware) operate independently of the CPU, generating pixel color assignments in real-time strictly dictated by the current raster position of the CRT beam.
3. Memory-Mapped State Representation (VRAM & PROMs): The signal generation hardware deterministically reads visual and audio state from specific memory architectures. Video RAM (VRAM) holds the mutable spatial layout (tile grid indices and sprite coordinate vectors). Graphic ROMs and Color PROMs hold the immutable 8x8 pixel bitmaps and color palettes, functioning as lookup tables for the hardware compositors.
4. Data Interconnect (System Bus): The physical 16-bit address bus and 8-bit data bus route binary data between the memory architecture and the processing core. This bus acts as the sole propagation vector for state mutations traveling from the execution core outward to the visual representation layer.
5. Execution and Timing Control (Z80 CPU & Interrupts): A Zilog Z80 microprocessor drives the system bus. Its execution cadence is causally locked to the hardware signal generation layer (Layer 2) via a Non-Maskable Interrupt (NMI). When the CRT raster sweep completes a frame (the V-blank interval), the timing hardware asserts the NMI, forcing the CPU to synchronize its execution cycles with the display hardware.
6. Application Logic (Software State Machines): The Z80 assembly instructions (stored in Program ROM) execute within the CPU to calculate game physics. This logic computes collision matrices, deterministically transitions ghost AI states, and updates coordinate vectors, utilizing Work RAM for volatile variables before pushing the final frame state across the system bus to VRAM.
7. Physical Input Polling (Electromechanical Interfaces): The initial causal trigger for non-deterministic state changes. The application logic polls specific memory- mapped addresses that are physically wired to microswitches in the joystick and coin mechanisms. Activating a switch pulls a hardware line low, altering the bitwise state read by the CPU logic and propagating downstream through the subsequent layers.

conversation.q: map the objects/mechanisms in each layer to game mechanics for a pacman-like game. we want to walk around and collect dots, but in a new environment that feels different for each layer and lets one experience its dynamics.
conversation.a:
Connecting the game world directly to a running Z80 emulator means the environment doesn't need scripted behavior—it is driven deterministically by the actual hardware state of the emulated machine.

Here is the mapping of each hardware layer into a playable, spatial grid mechanic:

**Layer 1: Analog Output Display (Cathode Ray Tube)**
Grid Topology: A 224x288 array of RGB phosphor triads (rotated 90 degrees to match the vertical monitor orientation of the cabinet). Collectibles (Dots): Decaying phosphor nodes. Because phosphor luminescence decays exponentially after excitation, a node is only collectible for a brief window after the electron beam passes over it. Environmental Hazard: The Raster Beam. A continuous, high-velocity hazard sweeping horizontally (H-sync) and stepping down vertically. Contact during an active scanline is fatal. Safe Windows: During Horizontal Blanking (H-blank) and Vertical Blanking (V-blank) intervals, the electron gun's voltage is suppressed to 0V while the magnetic deflection coils reset the beam's position. The player must time major vertical movements during the 60.6 Hz V-blank window when the beam retraces diagonally to the top-left without emitting lethal electrons. Emulator Coupling: Phosphor excitation intensity is mapped directly to the emulated video hardware's instantaneous RGB output pins.

**Layer 2: Hardware Signal Generation (Video/Audio Subsystems)**
Grid Topology: Two overlapping planes operating in parallel: the Static Tile Grid (28x36 cells of 8x8 pixels) and the Line Buffer Plane (which holds the 8 hardware sprites). Collectibles (Dots): Valid pixel color indices fetched from the Color PROM lookup tables before they are sent to the DAC. Environmental Hazard: Hardware Sprite Overlays & The WSG Audio Wave.
1. Up to 8 sprites per scanline materialize dynamically at the exact X/Y coordinates dictated by the emulator's Sprite RAM ( 0x4FF0–0x4FFF ). They act as moving crush hazards stamped onto the grid by the hardware compositor.
2. The Namco WSG (Waveform Sound Generator) reads frequency and volume registers ( 0x5040–0x505F ) to project a physical, oscillating waveform across the bottom of the grid. High-amplitude audio (e.g., the siren or death sound) expands the wave's bounding box, restricting player movement. Emulator Coupling: As the emulated Pac-Man eats dots in the base game, the corresponding background tiles in this layer change from dot bitmaps to empty space, physically altering the terrain geometry the player can traverse.

**Layer 3: Memory-Mapped State Representation (VRAM & PROMs)**
Grid Topology: The linear address space from 0x4000 to 0x47FF (1 KB of Video RAM and 1 KB of Color RAM), structured as a physical 2D memory array of 8-bit registers. Collectibles (Dots): Dirty bits—specific memory addresses that have been mutated since the last frame refresh. Environmental Hazard: Dual-Port Contention (Read/Write Collisions). The memory cells are constantly accessed by two independent entities:
1. The Video Hardware Reader: A deterministic, rhythmic sweep across the entire array that reads values to build the frame (non-lethal, pushes the player along).
2. The CPU Write Head: A localized, erratic hazard that teleports to specific addresses during the V-blank window and overwrites the byte values (lethal if the player occupies the target address during a write cycle). Emulator Coupling: The values written by the CPU Write Head are the actual hex values of the emulated game's VRAM updates. Changing a byte in Color RAM ( 0x4400– 0x47FF ) immediately alters the collision properties and color of that room on the grid.

**Layer 4: Data Interconnect (System Bus)**
Grid Topology: A high-speed routing network consisting of 16 parallel Address Lanes (unidirectional) intersecting with 8 parallel Data Lanes (bidirectional), gated by Control Lines ( /RD , /WR , /MREQ , /IORQ ). Collectibles (Dots): Floating payload bits ( 1 s) transmitted across the 8 data lanes. Environmental Hazard: High-Voltage Logic Transients & Tri-State Isolation. When the CPU asserts an address on the 16-bit bus, those specific lanes energize at 3.072 MHz. The player must read the active address binary pattern to predict which memory block (ROM, RAM, or I/O) is being targeted. When a device is not selected, its bus buffers enter a High-Impedance (Hi-Z) state, disconnecting bridges and isolating sections of the grid. Emulator Coupling: Every memory read or write executed by the Z80 emulator generates a corresponding physical packet wave on these lanes. During the game's attract mode vs. active gameplay, the traffic density and routing destinations shift noticeably.

**Layer 5: Execution and Timing Control (Z80 CPU & Interrupts)**
Grid Topology: The internal microarchitecture of the Zilog Z80: the Register File ( A , F , B , C , D , E , H , L , and their shadow registers), the Program Counter (PC), the Stack Pointer (SP), and the Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU). Collectibles (Dots): Status flags in the F register (Zero Z , Carry C , Sign S , Parity/Overflow P/V ) that spawn whenever the ALU completes an operation. Environmental Hazard: The Program Counter & The NMI Shockwave. The PC steps sequentially through instruction pipelines, acting as a relentless tracking entity. The NMI Reset: Every 16.5 milliseconds (60.6 Hz), the external video hardware asserts the Non-Maskable Interrupt pin. This triggers a system-wide event: current register states are violently pushed onto the Stack Pointer (SP) (creating falling block hazards in the Stack region), and the PC instantly warps to memory address 0x0066 , resetting the local loop topology. Emulator Coupling: The player experiences the exact instruction cycle (M-cycles and T-states) of the emulated Z80. Conditional jumps ( JP Z , JR NZ ) cause the pathways in front of the Program Counter to switch tracks in real time based on register values.

**Layer 6: Application Logic (Software State Machines)**
Grid Topology: The abstract 28x36 Logical Tile Map stored in Work RAM ( 0x4C00– 0x4FEF ). Unlike Layer 1 or 2, there are no pixels or sprites here—only raw coordinate vectors, bounding boxes, and mathematical target vectors. Collectibles (Dots): Unclaimed state variables and collision checks in the main game loop. Environmental Hazard: Deterministic Target-Tile Vectors. The four ghosts exist here not as graphic sprites, but as distinct mathematical targeting algorithms executing on the grid: Blinky ( 0x4920 ): Projects a direct Euclidean vector toward the emulated Pac- Man's current tile. Pinky: Projects a vector 4 tiles ahead of Pac-Man's orientation (including the famous overflow bug when facing Up, which shifts the vector 4 tiles Up and 4 tiles Left). Inky: Calculates a complex vector by doubling the distance line between Blinky's coordinates and 2 tiles ahead of Pac-Man. Clyde: Projects a direct vector until within an 8-tile Euclidean radius, at which point his vector snaps to the bottom-left corner (Scatter tile). Emulator Coupling: The player navigates inside the mathematical visualization of the ghost AI. When the global state timer transitions from Scatter to Chase, or when a Power Pellet sets the Frightened PRNG state, the vector beams sweeping the grid instantly recalculate their geometry.

**Layer 7: Physical Input Polling (Electromechanical Interfaces)**
Grid Topology: The memory-mapped input register IN0 ( 0x5000 ) and IN1 ( 0x5040 ), represented as a massive mechanical circuit board with 8 distinct tracks corresponding to the 8 bits of the input byte (Up, Down, Left, Right, Coin 1, Coin 2, Rack Advance, Service). Collectibles (Dots): Completed polling cycles—collecting the signal at the exact moment the Z80 CPU reads address 0x5000 during its V-blank input subroutine. Environmental Hazard: Active-Low Voltage Pulls & Contact Bounce. By default, pull-up resistors hold all 8 tracks at a lethal +5V (Logic High / 1 ). When the external player (or an automated input script) actuates a physical microswitch on the arcade cabinet, that specific track is connected to ground, dropping its voltage to 0V (Logic Low / 0 ) and creating a safe corridor to traverse. Contact Bounce: Because physical leaf switches vibrate for a few milliseconds upon closing, the track flickers rapidly between +5V and 0V before stabilizing, requiring precise timing to enter. Emulator Coupling: This layer bridges the player's physical controller to the emulator. Pressing "Left" on your physical controller grounds Bit 5 of 0x5000 , physically opening the "Left" corridor in Layer 7, which gets polled by the CPU in Layer 5, mutates the trajectory vector in Layer 6, travels across the bus in Layer 4, updates Sprite RAM in Layer 3, renders in Layer 2, and illuminates the CRT in Layer 1.
